Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

Copper prices spent most of August in a tight range of $100/t either side of $7500/t amid a summer lull in trading activity. Prices took their cues predominantly from macro data, although somewhat ironically, downward moves during the second half of the month were reversed in response to negative data; interpreted as being likely to raise the likelihood of new policy measures to stimulate faltering economic activity and hence copper demand, particularly in China and the US. 

**Trading dives as summer takes hold** August was expected to be a quiet month on the trading front given the absence of many market participants in the northern hemisphere amid summer vacations.  Both traded volume and open interest declined accordingly as most traders remained on the sidelines to avoid getting caught out in thin volumes.  Interestingly, analysis of open interest and price moves revealed that in the first full week of trading in August new longs had entered the market for the first time since the end of March.  Market sentiment, and, as a consequence, prices have softened since March, broadly as a result of renewed European sovereign debt and demand fears.  This led to a predominance of long liquidation and new shorts over this period, interspersed by the occasional short covering rally.  With this in mind, it seemed strange then that new longs were in the ascendency, although given the thin volumes only a small increase in prices/open interest was needed to cause this reaction. 

**Macro news causing moves** As with the previous month, price movements tended to be in response to macroeconomic news, rather than any significant fundamental developments for copper.  Indeed, there has been something of a “will they…won’t they…” mood across various corners of financial markets of late and it was disappointment over a lack of action from the ECB on bond purchasing that sent copper prices lower at the start of August.  Prices quickly rallied back up to $7600/t on hopes of a decisive resolution to Europe’s debt travails, while at the same time there were indications of economic support by policymakers in the US and in China.  Despite this prices ebbed lower from the 8<sup>th</sup> of the month as a string of broadly negative data emerged from China, which pulled prices down to the $7400/t level by the 13<sup>th</sup> .  After a few days of price inactivity cash quotes began yet another sedentary climb after a slew of downbeat comments from Chinese officials were viewed as suggesting a growing need for additional economic stimulation.  At the same time the euro was strengthening against the greenback, first on comments from German Chancellor Angela Merkel, giving public support for the ECB’s efforts to solve the regional debt crisis.  Prices were then bolstered by renewed rumours that the ECB was drawing up plans to ease

**Turning to China** The release of Chinese trade data temporarily switched the focus away from macro news and caught many in the market by surprise. Most market observers had been forecasting a decline in Chinese imports “next month” for most of the year but it was not until June that import quantities began to follow this script. In truth, a modest c.4kt rise on the prior month to 254kt in July can hardly be viewed as bucking a downward trend, although the rise in Chilean exports to China in June had already indicated that a major fall in overall Chinese metal imports during July was unlikely. The majority of imports had been ascribed to contract purchases and financing, however, our discussions with market participants revealed that while the market as a whole had been (and still is) relatively quiet, there has been some demand for spot purchases of cathode. This is not just for financing purposes, nor is it piling up in bonded warehouses. More recently, other indicators that might suggest improved spot activity in China moving forward include, rising Metals Market Service Monthly Update - August 2012 Page 2 of 22 Copper Monthly Update cancelled warrants in nearby Asian LME registered warehouses and the SHFE moving into backwardation. However, it must also be noted that Jinchuan are reportedly in the market for cathode to replace lost secondary output as we discuss in the _Production_ section of this report. We understand that bonded warehouse stocks remained at around the 600kt level, with the same amount withdrawn as went in. Our estimates of shipments into bonded warehouses suggests that less material went in than in previous months, suggesting at first sight that imported material was for real use and thus pointing to improving demand. However, refined production fell month-on-month in July as a result of smelter maintenance shutdowns, including the 400kt/a Xiangguang plant, and so more likely it would appear that imports were simply making up for lost domestic production. Looking at the impact of imports and output on apparent consumption calculations, the July figure of 684kt is the lowest level this year. But given that apparent consumption was bloated by imports in the first half of the year and did not reflect the true level of demand then, there needs to be a tipping point where real demand overtakes apparent consumption in the second half. We have been saying all year that demand in China will pick up in H2 and we remain of that view, no

t least because the commissioning of some major semis projects will at the very least displace imports of semis and in doing so boost domestic refined demand. Meanwhile, the downbeat tone of the HSBC flash China PMI paints a darker picture than we are forecasting in terms of current and future demand. It is important to note that this index covers private enterprises and does not include the state owned enterprises that are benefiting and will further gain from rising momentum in infrastructure spending and the large government contracts associated with this. Contradictory data is often a feature of turning points and given that there is so much of it right now, it might just indicate that we are at a crossroads for Chinese consumption. #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 800 450

**Paying the premium for European material** Premia remained in line with last month in China in the $50-$75/t range and thus adding no new information to either the bullish or bearish argument for supply and demand in that country. Meanwhile, a rise in premia in Europe was certainly not a reflection of the current sluggish state of demand in the region amid extended summer shutdowns at semis producers, but rather due to the shortage of available inventories. Stocks in local LME warehouses are low, while shipments into the region have also been delayed. There are also rumours that South American cathode destined for Europe has been diverted to North America. All these factors combined to push premia up around $80-90/t. In the US, premia have been elevated for some time amid a shortage of truck drivers and the maintenance shutdown at the Kennecott smelter. Levels are consistent with last month at 6-7c/lb, despite Kennecott being back in production as it catches up on prior orders. Demand in the US seems to be bumping along without decisively moving higher, although we understand that there has been an uptick in enquiries for material amid declining inventories ahead of the seasonal Autumn upturn. **North American withdrawals pull global stocks lower** Total exchange stocks across the LME, SHFE and COMEX have ebbed lower over the past month, with withdrawals from LME warehouses accounting for the fall. In fact, COMEX stocks have edged higher this month to 46kt from 44kt at the end of last month, while SHFE stocks have also crept up to 159kt from 157kt at the close of July. Material in LME sheds was relatively stable in Europe at 15kt, while inventories in Asia edged slightly lower, although interestingly, there has been a rise in cancelled warrants in Asia over the past couple of months. Thi

s adds a little weight to what we are hearing about improving spot demand from China as the assumed destination for these cancellations. However, it was a decline in North American warehouses that accounted for the fall in total LME stocks, with regional inventories down from 121kt last month to 112kt currently. This puts material held in LME warehouses at 234kt as of 28th of August compared to 249kt at the end of July. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - August 2012 Page 3 of 22 Copper Monthly Update **Olympic failure for Australia…** Amongst the raft of quarterly results this month, the general impression has been that mines have continued to fall short of production expectations, most notably in Chile and, to a lesser extent in Zambia and the DRC. One major piece of news came from the BHP Billiton camp with the announcement that it had shelved the planned expansion at Olympic Dam in South Australia. Although not altogether unsurprising, it was viewed in some quarters as supportive of current prices on the basis it would serve to tighten the market. However, this project was envisaged to be in three stages, the first of which we had expected to come into production in 2017 at a rate of 170kt/a. Therefore, the shelving of this project will not alter our near-term view of mine supply or copper prices. That said an expansion at Olympic Dam is by no means dead given BHP Billiton’s announcement that it would review alternative, less capital intensive designs for the project. #### **Copper spot premia ($/t)** 180 10

**…but mine project approvals continue apace…** Given BHP Billiton’s announcement and the general erosion of risk appetite, there is a growing feeling in the marketplace that many mine projects have been deferred while those under development are now relatively few in number. This is, in fact, not true as there is little evidence of firm announcements of project cancellations or deferrals to date. Moreover, there have been a number of project approvals so far this year. Noteworthy inclusions being Cobre Panama, Constancia, the Cerro Verde mill expansion, Sentinel, Pinto Valley restart and the Morenci expansion (and Antucoya at the end of last year). These will more than offset the loss of the Olympic Dam expansion and are in addition to major projects that are coming on stream this year and over the next 24 months including Antapaccay, Antucoya, Cadia East, Caserones, DeGrussa, Oyu Tolgoi, Miheevskoye, MMH (Codelco), Salobo and Sierra Gorda. Meanwhile, significant brownfield expansions are underway at Antamina, Chino restart, Gibraltar, Kansanshi, KOV, Mutanda and Wunugetu

shan (which will be China’s second largest copper mine after Dexing). On this basis, any belief out there in the market of a lack of new projects coming through does appear to be somewhat misguided. **…as do disruptions** Although Olympic Dam does not provide a compelling near term argument for price support, the same can not be said of the level of disruptions to mine supply so far this year. After having digested the latest quarterly releases from mining companies, we have now used up 3.4% of our 5% disruption allowance, which equates to some 600kt of lost output this year. The major losses are accounted for by technical problems at mines, the slow ramp up of projects and lower than expected ore grades. Interestingly, strikes have accounted for very little lost production so far. On a regional basis, South America accounts for just over half of all disruptions. The persistent nature of these disruptions over the past eight years fully justifies our ongoing use of a 5% generic mine disruption allowance at the start of each year in our supply forecasts that is eroded over time when specific mine losses are identified. **Q4 upturn reiterated** Our forecasts for this year have been largely built on the premise of recovering Chinese demand in the second half of 2012 and this continues to be the case. There are a number of factors pointing to improving activity in China which we have outlined above, including rising interest in cathode in the spot market and an expansion in semis production in the final part of the year. It is important to note that even without sequential improvements in consumption from Q3 to Q4, year-on-year growth will be flattered by the favourable comparison with the final three months of 2011, which were particularly weak. Moreover, even if China’s production of semis takes demand away from elsewhere, such that there is no net gain in overall semis output, the positive impact on sentiment that increased Chinese demand has, will surely be supportive of prices. The key question for prices is of course the extent to which this will be met from stocks or by imports, the latter which would likely provide the most powerful signal to the market of recovering demand in China. In line with our forecast improvement in Chinese consumption and continued tightness in supply, we expect prices will climb from current levels to average $8000/t in the fourth quarter and $7937/t for the year as a whole. ## Consumption 

This year global copper consumption has been particularly subdued over the late summer months.  Faced with generally lacklustre end use markets European fabricators have chosen to moderately extend their usual summer shutdowns and await the resumption of business in September.  But with the region’s economic turmoil still unresolved there appears only limited scope for the seasonal upturn.  North American volumes are acceptable, if unspectacular, with hopes still pinned on the construction sector as it inches out of recession.  Japanese wire and cable shipments rose 9% year-onyear in July, the best monthly performance to date this year, however, this was largely offset by a 6% year-on-year drop in brass mill output.  In China, the expected improvement in copper power cable orders has still to fully materialise. Capacity utilisation in the wire and cable industry rose in August but this has not yet resulted in higher orders for rod mills as cablemakers are working through existing stocks to meet the initial increase.  If the influx is sustained then rod mills should see the benefit in September and October. 

### **Western Europe** 

**Consumers extend holiday / maintenance shutdowns** Amid the increasingly uncertain economic climate many consumers have opted to slightly extend their traditional late summer shutdowns in line with faltering demand in their end user industries.  This has varied from just a few extra days in the case of some, to a week or more for others, depending on the national market and the spectrum of end use sectors served.  Construction markets have been most affected by this loss of momentum.  The first quarter had seen volumes supported by a mild winter, but the second quarter was softer with the usual seasonal upturn arriving later and with less force in northern European markets, but not at all in depressed southern European countries.  Italian and Spanish demand for building wire deteriorated in the second quarter and there are no indications that this trend will be arrested during the third quarter. 

**Utility power cable demand slows…** Orders from p

ower utilities for distribution cables (for new build, repair and maintenance, and renewable energy projects) weakened in the second quarter except for the healthy markets of France and the Nordic countries.  In Germany, regulatory uncertainties are contributing to the slowdown in project execution.  As an example, the German power utility RWE recently postponed its investment decision on the €3Bn Innogy Nordsee I offshore wind farm from the second half of 2012 until at least early 2013.  At present the German government has made no revenue guarantees to wind farm owners or network operators.  This has delayed the construction of power lines to connect the remotely generated power sources to the grid, which has in turn made wind farm investors more wary of commencing their own projects with the infrastructure funding question still unresolved.  The issue is a pressing one with Germany intending to phase out all its nuclear plants by 2022 and replace them with 10,000MW of wind power capacity on its North Sea and Baltic Sea coasts. 

**…and aluminium takes a greater share** The utility power cable business in France has always been heavily biased towards aluminium conductors.  However, there is a now a clear trend across Europe towards the substitution of copper power cables by aluminium in both utility and industrial applications.  In the past, the European cable industry had adopted a more neutral stance towards conductor choice but there has been a steady shift in favour of offering more cost effective solutions (i.e. aluminium) in the current business environment.  Aluminium is now also gaining share in the submarine power cable market, a sector previously and exclusively the preserve of copper designs for ease of handling at sea. 

**Copper wire rod volumes suffer and competition intensifies** With regional volumes down an estimated 10-15% year-on-year in H1 2012, mills have steadily adopted a more aggressive attitude in the export market to offset declining volumes in their home market.  Exports of rod and drawn wire from Italy, Spain, Sweden and Poland all increased yearon-year in H1 2012 while Kazakhmys’ German subsidiary MKM also claimed higher sales based on the attractiveness of its tolling business.  By comparison FYQ3 rod output by European industry leader and major exporter Aurubis fell 22% to 155kt from 199kt a year ago.  The company said that although it had continued to see strong demand from the automotive sector (as evidenced by wiring harness assembler Leoni’s healthy Q2 results), orders from cablemakers and enamelled wire producers had declined, especially in southern Europe.  Italian copper wire rod output only fell 4% to 224kt in H1 2012, aided by a 23% surge in exports of rod and drawn wire. 

**Brass mills also facing an uphill struggle** The European market for copper and alloy tubes, rod and bars, and flat rolled products has endured depressed demand throughout 2012.  With construction activity subdued and the HVACR secto

r and industrial manufacturing also contracting, it has only been the automotive and the electrical distribution equipment industries that have offered some opportunities. Commercial tube demand is, if anything, even weaker than copper plumbing tube across the European market. Brass rod sales have been hit both by the weak construction market and low industrial demand. Copper bar and section demand for bus bar and electrical distribution equipment is stable. Interconnect offtake for the auto sector is healthy but all other areas of the flat rolled products business are slack. KME reported that its total sales of brass mill products dropped 15% year-on-year in H1 2012. Total Italian production of brass mill products fell 10% to 315kt in H1 2012 according to data from ASSOMET. ### **USA** **Consumption holds firm** Although the United States economy slowed in the second quarter, we still expect refined consumption of copper to increase by 1% this year. GDP grew at an annual rate of 1.5% from April to June, slightly lower than the 2% increase over the first three months of the year. The second quarter slowdown was not entirely surprising amid weak consumer spending, government cuts and a rise in imports from foreign countries. Consumer expenditure slowed to 1.5%, down from 2.4% in the first quarter, as households remain cautious on spending, particularly on big-ticket items like automobiles, as well as smaller items like clothing and groceries. Government cuts, especially at the state and local level, also weighed on growth. On a more positive note, spending by businesses improved as they increased their purchases of equipment and software to a 7.2% annual rate. Expectations are for an improvement in economic growth in the second half of the year. The housing market has recently shown signs of recovery, which could translate into more construction jobs and consumer spending. Although major automakers reported U.S. auto sales for July were softer than expected as unemployment and weak consumer confidence kept would-be buyers on the sidelines, industry sales are due to jump 9% to 1.1 million vehicles. Sales early on in the year exceeded the most bullish forecasts, but since May, the rate of improvement has started to ease, with the July sales figures showing a continuation of the slowdown. However, with the introduction of new models in the second half of the year, automakers anticipate a pick up in sales, with indications for August looking promising. **Mueller Industries in labour contrac

t negotiations** The unionised employees of Mueller Copper Tube of Fulton are currently in a contract disagreement with management.  The members of United Steelworkers Local 8420, a labour union that represents more than 260 employees of Mueller Copper Tube, have rejected the company’s latest employment contract.  The previous agreement, which expired on 1<sup>st</sup> August 2012, has been extended for 90 days.  This period is intended to give the two groups time to negotiate a new agreement.  Before the 90 day period ends, members of the trade union must vote again to decide if they accept the new collective bargaining agreement.  At the present time it is unclear whether the employees rejection of the company’s proposal will lead to either another extension and negotiation period or a strike.  Additional union contracts that are due for renewal this year include those at the company’s facilities at North Wales, Pennsylvania (3<sup>rd</sup> August), Belding, Michigan (15<sup>th</sup> August) and Waynesboro, Tennessee (7<sup>th</sup> November). 

**Dollar coin debate dents profits** The debate about the dollar coin in the USA continues.  The introduction the US Presidential coins series has not been a success.  In 2005, Congress enacted the Presidential $1 Coin Act, which mandated that the Mint issue four new presidential dollar coins each year from 2007 to 2016.  However, demand has not met supply.  At the end of 2011 the Treasury Department announced a decision to stop mass production of presidential dollar coins.  The view is that this will save the government money, around $50 million annually over the next several years according to the Deputy Secretary of the Treasury, given that the US Mint has produced $1.4 billion in surplus dollar coins that are sitting in Federal Reserve vaults.  While there are both positives and negatives to the argument for a dollar coin instead of the dollar bill, the decision by the Treasury to cease production of the dollar coin for general circulation has resulted in a dent in profits at some producers of flat rolled products.  Should any decision be made to introduce dollar coins instead of the $1 bill, this would certainly support demand for copper.  Legislation was introduced at both the House and the Senate that would replace the dollar bill with the $1 coin during Q1 this year.  It remains to be seen if this is adopted, despite the preference for the dollar bill.  Meanwhile Global Brass and Copper Holdings Inc. highlighted in its latest quarterly report that on a consolidated basis sales volumes were down by around 4.7% year-on-

**Brass mill shipments show tentative improvement** Total shipments of brass mill products remain weak so far this year, with total shipments recording a 3% decline in the year to May 2012 compared to the same period last year. However total shipments are slowly starting to recover with the May data showing a 0.9% increase year-on-year, the first positive monthly increase on a year-to-year basis.  Shipments of copper rod, bars and sections and copper tubes continue to suffer, down 8.4% and 11.9% respectively in the year to May year-on-year.  In contrast, shipments of copper plate, sheet and strip grew by 3.9% over the same period.  Meanwhile shipments of copper alloy rod, bars and sections and copper alloy plate, sheet and strip are showing some improvement, benefitting from the slow recovery in the construction sector and automotive sectors.  Copper alloy tube shipments, which account for a very small share of the market, remain very weak, and are down 27.6% in the year to May. 

**Wire & cable companies profits show modest increase** Two large wire & cable manufacturers General Cable and Nexans indicated in their latest quarterly reports that sales volumes and revenues continue to suffer from the global industrial slowdown.  General Cable’s net sales for Q2 2012 were $1.478 billion, an increase of $66.6 million, or 5%, compared to the second quarter of 2011 on a metal-adjusted basis.  Volumes based on metal pounds sold increased 5% in the second quarter of 2012 compared to 2011 principally due to the ongoing strength in global aerial transmission product shipments (aluminium).  Sequentially, volume based on metal pounds sold increased 2% principally due to demand in France and the Mediterranean as well as stable demand in most ROW and North American businesses as compared to the first quarter.  However, General Cable highlighted that demand for its wire and cable products stalled during Q2 2012 in parts of the Company’s North America segment.  Meanwhile a relatively mild winter and stronger wind farm activity may have pulled forward demand into the first quarter for electric utility distribution cables in North America. The decline of metal prices, of both copper and aluminium also affected the buying behaviour of rod mill customers and distributors, while the ongoing uncertainty had delayed certain projects.  Overall sales of metal in North America rose in Q2 2012 to 85.8 million lbs up from 84.4 million lbs in Q2 2011 and 84.6 million lbs in Q1 2012.  Revenues also rose, due to the strong performance of the Company’s telephone and electric utility businesses as well as specialty cables used in natural resource extraction applications.  The Company announced on May 21st that it agree

d to acquire Alcan Cable, the aluminium wire and cable business of Rio Tinto plc for $185 million in cash.  The manufacturing and distribution facilities service energy and construction markets in the United States, Canada, Mexico, and China.  The deal is due to be concluded in the second half of 2012, subject to receipt of regulatory approval.  In early June, General Cable said that it agreed to acquire a majority interest (60%) in Procables S.A. of Colombia for $45 million.  Procables has two manufacturing facilities in Bogota and Barranquilla with a broad range of wire and cable products, including low and medium voltage power cables, building wire, industrial, communications, and bare aluminium conductors as well as operating copper and aluminium rod mills.  The transaction is also expected to be agreed in the second half of 2012, subject to receipt of regulatory approval. 

Nexans sales for the first half of 2012 totalled 3.58 billion euros compared with 3.53 billion euros for the first half of 2011. At constant non-ferrous metal prices, sales amount to 2.40 billion euros compared with 2.29 billion euros for the first half of 2011, a 0.2% increase in organic growth, however excluding Transmission, growth increased 3.4% year-on-year. Meanwhile, Nexans has started the construction of its first high voltage power cable manufacturing plant in North America in June 2012 with an initial investment of $85 million in Berkeley County, in Charleston, South Carolina.  The first phase of the facility will focus on the manufacture of underground power cables up to extra high voltage (EHV) levels of 500 kV.  The plant will begin operation in 2014 and will enable the company to make the most of the increasing demand for high voltage cables designed and manufactured to meet the needs of the major power transmission infrastructure projects planned in North America and worldwide in the coming years. During August Chinese No.2 scrap spreads widened slightly to around 3,650Rmb/t (26 c/lb) compared to 3,300 RMB/t (24c/lb) during July  After slipping to 33c/lb under the 3-month COMEX price at the end of July, the No. 2 scrap spread recovered to average 36c/lb during August. 

**Japanese smelter to recover precious metals** Mitsubishi Materials announced a JPY1.7Bn ($22M) investment in a facility to recover precious metals from 20kt/a of scrap at its Onahama smelter.  The company is looking to boost profitability at the operation that has been impacted by low TCRCs for treating concentrates and low utilisation of its existing scrap process line which is designed to process shredder dusts.  The availability of feed stock generated by shredding cars is reported to be limited as second hand vehicles are diverted to parts of the country impacted by last years Tsunami.  Current government initiatives to promote new car sales are expected to increase the availability of shredder dust in the short term. 

**Smelter scrap scarce in Japan** Reports from Japan suggest that the country’s smelters are facing a shortage of smelter grade scrap.  Suppressed metal prices and low levels of building redevelopment have restricted the supply of scrap to smelters who require secondary feed in order to maintain production rates in the face of falling concentrate grades.  Smelter grade scrap, containing about 95% copper was reported to be trading at wholesale prices in the range 500-510 y/kg (289 to 295c/lb) with some buyers paying a 10 to 15 y/kg (6 to 9c/lb) premium.  Japanese smelter production from secondary materials and re-smelted blister is forecast to be ~240kt in 2012. 

**Jinchuan looking to buy cathodes to cover scrap shortfall** Jinchuan’s plans to produce 600kt of cathodes this year are unlikely to materialise due to tightening scrap supplies, narrowing spreads and the long distances involved in shipping this material to its smelter in Gansu province and the resulting cathode back to markets in the east of the country.  According to some reports the company may be in the market for 150kt of cathodes during August and September in order to cover commitments that it cannot make from its own facilities.  However, these reports appear to exaggerate the likely outcome as Jinchuan’s overall secondary production is 200kt/a, implying the company has been unable to source the equivalent of 9 month’s of scrap feed, which seems unlikely.  Any requirement for metal is more likely to be met from bonded warehouse stocks than from a boost in imports. 

**Blister market static** Activity on the spot blister market remained sparse with material secur

ed through long-term contracts appearing sufficient to satisfy buyers’ requirements thus far this year.  RCs sought by Chinese buyers have been around $90/t, while European terms have remained at the $100/t level or higher, seen in previous months.

## Production news 

**Disappointing first half mine production in Chile** According to statistics from the Chilean Copper Commission (COCHILCO), the country’s copper mine production for the first six months of 2012 was 2.625Mt.  Although this figure was over 2% higher than that achieved in the first half of 2011, the total was lower than previously anticipated with incremental output from new production capability not meeting initial forecasts and some established producers operating significantly below last year’s levels.  As reported last month, low grades, adverse weather, safety stoppages and technical problems saw first half production at Collahuasi limited to 145kt, 38% down on 2011.  Meanwhile, commercial production reported by Codelco for the first half of 2012 was 767kt, 6.3% lower than the equivalent period during 2011 with the shortfall being attributable to reduced production from the company’s operations in the north of Chile where reduced ore grades, unsettled labour relations and an unscheduled smelter outage meant that combined output from Chuquicamata and Radomiro Tomic amounted to 359kt compared to 436kt in the first half of 2011.  First half production from the expanded Los Bronces mine was 183kt. Although this output was 80% higher than the first six months of 2011, Anglo American reported that a strong ramp up in ore throughput that saw 92% of nameplate capacity achieved, had been offset by lower than forecast head grades, low recoveries and adverse weather.  Combined first half recoverable production reported by Freeport for its Candelaria and Ojos Del Salado mines was 65kt, down by 23% on the first six months of 2011 due to anticipated lower head grades. 

**Peruvian production increase** Statistics from the Peruvian Ministry of Energy and Mines showed the country’s first half mined copper production rose to 611kt in the first half of 2012, a 3.7% increase on the equivalent period in 2011.  The major contributor to this increase was the Antamina mine where the $1.3bn expansion in mill throughput from 95kt/d to 130kt/d is ramping up and H1 production of 202kt was 39% higher than 2011.  Mitigating this rise were mines reporting lower production, in

particular Freeport’s majority-owned Cerro Verde mine where recoverable copper production in H1 was 132kt, 16% down on the first six months of 2011 due to anticipated lower head grades and Xstrata’s Tintaya mine that is scheduled to be depleted this year and where overall H1 output of 20kt was less than half of that achieved in 2011.  The official statistics showed that overall output from Sociedad Minera El Brocal’s Colquijirca operations was just 6.7kt during the first half of 2012, compared to 11.8kt during the first six months of 2011.  With the copper circuit at the La Oroya smelter remaining out of action and the Tsumeb smelter in Namibia operating at reduced capacity, Peru’s smaller mines producing concentrates with an elevated arsenic content are understood to be finding it difficult to find buyers for their output. 

**Xstrata look to projects for second half recovery** Xstrata reported mined copper production for the first six months of 2012 of 355kt, 18% lower than the equivalent period in 2011.  As mentioned, lower production from Collahuasi, caused by low grades, adverse weather, safety stoppages and technical problems, meant that Xstrata’s share of total output from the Chilean mine was 64kt compared to 103kt in the first half of 2011.  First half production at Tintaya in Peru, which is in its final year of operation was just 20kt, 52% lower than 2011, however the company reported that development of the neighbouring Antapaccay project, rated to produce 160kt/a of copper in concentrate, was on schedule to start operations in Q3.  Output from the Australian Ernest Henry mine was 15kt compared to 55kt during the same period in 2011 as the operation continued to transition to underground mining. During the second half of the year feed to the Ernest Henry mill will be supplemented by ore from the new Mount Margaret open pit that is forecast to contribute 30kt/a to overall output.  Xstrata’s share of production from the newly expanded Antamina mine was 68kt, up by 39% on 2011. 

**Grupo Mexico expansions underway** Grupo Mexico announced copper sales for the first half of 2012 of 427kt, a 13% increase on the equivalent period in 2011, attributable to improved head grades particularly at its Ray, Cuajone and La Caridad operations.  The company also provided an update on expansion projects currently in progress:  A $1.4Bn mill expansion at the Buenavista mine in Mexico rated to add 188kt/a of copper in concentrate production is in construction and reported to be on schedule to start production in the second half of 2015, while commissioning of the $444M SxEw III project at the same mine, rated to add 120kt/a of cathode production capacity is targeted for the second half of 2014. Meanwhile in Peru, the company is investing in new crushers and conveyors to replace the existing rail haulage systems at Toquepala and Cuajone. It is understood that regulatory approval for projects to increase production at these mines is still being sought.
